title: Professionals and field-level change: Institutional work and the professional project
author: Roy Suddaby · Thierry Viale

dom.t: Professional authority: AI enters an already contested field

mo.t: Elite renewal: Innovation can reproduce legal power

kp.k: Professional projects drive institutional change from within
kp.d: Suddaby and Viale argue that changes in professional jurisdictions are causally connected to changes in organizational fields because professional projects incorporate projects of institutionalization. Their theoretical contribution positions the professional project as an endogenous mechanism of institutional change, rather than making a claim about AI or legal services specifically.
qs: This article explicates the causal connections between changes in professional jurisdictions and changes in organizational fields.
The authors argue that professional projects carry within them projects of institutionalization.
The key contribution of this article is to explicate the professional project as an endogenous mechanism of institutional change.

kp.k: Professionals perform critical but often invisible institutional work
kp.d: The authors identify professionals as agents in the creation, maintenance and transformation of institutions. This framing encompasses sustaining institutions as well as changing them.
qs: They focus attention on the critical but often invisible role that professionals play in institutional work, or the creation, maintenance and transformation of institutions.

kp.k: Four dynamics derive from reviewing prior research
kp.d: The four-dynamic account of professional field reconfiguration is based on a review of prior institutional-change research in which professionals play a central role. The supplied document explicitly characterizes the evidentiary base as neither a case study nor new data.
qs: Based on a review of prior research on institutional change in which professionals play a central role, the authors observe four essential dynamics through which professionals reconfigure institutions and organizational fields.
Not a case study, and no new data.

kp.k: Expertise and legitimacy open new professional spaces
kp.d: The first dynamic involves professionals deploying expertise and legitimacy to challenge the incumbent order and define a new, open and uncontested space.
qs: First, professionals use their expertise and legitimacy to challenge the incumbent order and to define a new, open and uncontested space.

kp.k: Social capital introduces new actors and identities
kp.d: The second dynamic concerns professionals using their inherent social capital and skill to populate a field with new actors and new identities.
qs: Second, professionals use their inherent social capital and skill to populate the field with new actors and new identities.

kp.k: New rules and standards recreate field boundaries
kp.d: The third dynamic identifies professionals' introduction of nascent rules and standards as a mechanism for recreating the boundaries of an organizational field.
qs: Third, professionals introduce nascent new rules and standards that recreate the boundaries of the field.

kp.k: Managing social capital establishes new status hierarchies
kp.d: The fourth dynamic concerns professionals managing the use and reproduction of social capital within a field, thereby conferring a new status hierarchy or social order.
qs: Fourth, professionals manage the use and reproduction of social capital within a field thereby conferring a new status hierarchy or social order within the field.

pts.k: Suddaby and Viale argue that professionals change organizational fields through their professional projects; the supplied source makes no claims about AI or AI-driven legal change.
pts.d: In this cross-domain account, the authors identify professional projects as an endogenous mechanism of institutional change connecting shifts in professional jurisdictions to shifts in organizational fields. They specify four dynamics: professionals deploy expertise and legitimacy to challenge incumbents and establish new spaces; use social capital and skill to introduce actors and identities; introduce rules and standards that redraw field boundaries; and manage social capital to establish new status hierarchies. These are general explanatory claims about professional field reconfiguration, not technology forecasts.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The four-dynamic account is based on a review of prior research on institutional change involving professionals.
pts.d: The authors present a conceptual synthesis of existing research. The accompanying document description explicitly characterizes the evidence base as neither a new case study nor new data. The supplied abstract does not identify individual studies, datasets, quantitative estimates, or tests of the proposed causal mechanisms.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The 2011 source offers a general mechanism of change without a forecast horizon or specified duration.
pts.d: The account concerns institutional change in which professionals play a central role. Its mechanisms involve professionals exercising expertise, legitimacy, skill, social capital, and influence over rules and standards. The abstract does not specify when these dynamics arise, how quickly they operate, or whether the four dynamics must occur in a fixed temporal sequence. Publication in 2011 is bibliographic context, not a prediction deadline.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Professionals, incumbent field participants, and new actors are implicated in changes to jurisdictions, identities, boundaries, and status hierarchies.
pts.d: Professionals are portrayed as active creators, maintainers, and transformers of institutions. Incumbent orders are challenged; new actors and identities enter the field; rules and standards reshape boundaries; and the management of social capital produces a new social order. The supplied text does not distinguish particular professions, legal-market segments, firm types, clients, or public beneficiaries.
